I'm Tanuja, and I was the youngest on the team when the soap campaign flopped.
Nobody said it was my fault. Not out loud. But in the review meeting, Thomas, our lead, said, “Some of the copy wasn't quite on brand,” and looked at my slides. Everyone else looked at me too.

The open-air concert in Madrid was packed shoulder to shoulder. Clara and Javier were twenty metres from the stage when someone near them shouted, “Fight! There's a fight!”
Nobody could see a fight. But people started to turn and push. The push rolled through the crowd like a wave. Clara's feet left the ground for a second. Her arms were pinned. She couldn't breathe properly.
“Clara, arms up!” Javier shouted. She lifted her arms in front of her chest. They let the wave carry them sideways instead of fighting it.
A steward opened a side gate and people spilled out onto the grass. Clara sat down, shaking and furious. “There wasn't even a fight,” she said. “Just a shout.”

Dear Jeevan bhaiya,
I'm writing because I still can't talk about it without my hands shaking.
At the temple festival on Saturday, near the main gate, the crowd was so thick we could barely move. Then someone said the gates were closing. They weren't. But everyone surged forward at once. I was pushed from every side. My dupatta got pulled off. I lost Amma's hand for almost a minute.
I remember thinking, it isn't one person hurting me. It's all of us together. Nobody was bad. The crowd was.
A policeman on a platform finally shouted that the gate was open till midnight, and the pushing slowed.
I'm angry at whoever started the rumour, and angry there were no announcements.
Jyoti

At the railway station exit this evening, the crowd grew dense very fast after two trains arrived together. I watched Gautam, one of our older scouts, very closely.

New Year's Eve, 2 am
Big concert at the beach tonight. Before it started, I made Vishal walk the edges with me. He rolled his eyes, but we found three exits and agreed: if we get separated, meet at the lifeguard tower.
At midnight, the fireworks went up and the crowd pushed towards the stage. Suddenly we were squashed. Vishal started pushing back, panicking. I grabbed his arm. “Arms up, like me. Don't fight it. Go with it, sideways.” We edged left, towards the second exit, step by step.
We got out onto the sand, breathing hard. Behind us, people were still pressed together.
I'm still shaky, but proud. Having a plan made me calm when it mattered.
Ishita

qa.a: He was probably panicking and frightened, and then relieved when Ishita gave clear instructions.

Tushar's phone buzzed during his lunch break in the Bengaluru office. A viral post: a café owner in Indiranagar slapping a delivery boy, with the café's name in the caption. Two thousand shares in an hour. His finger hovered over share. He was furious.
Then he stopped. Something about the video looked off. The signs in the background weren't in Kannada or English.
He spent four minutes searching. The same clip had been posted three years ago from another country. The café in the caption had nothing to do with it.
He texted Preeti, who had already shared it. “Check this, it's fake. Wrong café.” Preeti replied, “Oh no. Deleting.” Tushar posted the original link under the viral post. By evening, the café owner's reply was pinned at the top.

I'm Mohit, and one evening last year, I nearly helped start something terrible.
A video came into our colony group: a man in a cap walking near the school, and a message saying he was a child kidnapper, with a photo of a local vegetable seller who looked a bit similar. People were furious. Someone wrote, “Let's find him tonight.”
My cousin Jaya had already forwarded it to two more groups. My thumb was on forward too.
Then I stopped. I searched the words of the message. The same text had been going round in three other states, with different photos. The police page had a notice calling it false.
I posted the police notice in the group and called Jaya. She deleted her forwards. The vegetable seller was at his cart the next morning, safe.
